projectDesc.p: The Welte-Mignon Advertisements Collection brings together print advertisements for the Welte-Mignon reproducing piano that appeared between 1905 and 1930. It was created as part of the PhD project "Grünfelds Geist" at the University of Tübingen, which considers piano rolls as objects of a digital edition. The collection is published at https://anz.welte225.org.

samplingDecl.p: The collection gathers print advertisements for the Welte-Mignon reproducing piano that appeared between 1905 and 1930 and were published by M. Welte & Söhne, by one of its licensees, or by a dealer or agent selling the instrument. Each advertisement is encoded once; its further printings, in the same or in other periodicals, are listed as further sources.

The advertisements were found in digitised newspapers and magazines: Chronicling America (Library of Congress), the British Newspaper Archive, HathiTrust (copies of the Universities of California, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota and Virginia), the Internet Archive, the Digitale Sammlungen of the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, ANNO (Austrian National Library), the International Arcade Museum Library, Georgia Historic Newspapers, Delpher (KB, National Library of the Netherlands), eluxemburgensia (National Library of Luxembourg), RetroNews (Bibliothèque nationale de France), the archives of Le Temps, the Nasjonalbiblioteket of Norway, Mediestream (Royal Danish Library), the National Library of Latvia (through Europeana), Canadiana, the Hemeroteca Nacional Digital de México, the St Petersburg State Theatre Library, Trove (National Library of Australia), the newspapers of the Kungliga biblioteket of Sweden, e-newspaperarchives.ch, BAnQ numérique (Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec), the Biblioteca Virtual de Prensa Histórica, the archive of ABC, ARCA (Biblioteca de Catalunya) and Polona (National Library of Poland).

editorialDecl.p: Each file transcribes one printing of an advertisement, the one whose scan its facsimile zones refer to; decls on text points to its sourceDesc. The further printings were identified as the same advertisement but not collated word for word; differences that were noticed are recorded with app, whose first rdg is that of the transcribed printing, or in a note. A printing that was set anew counts as the same advertisement as long as its text differs only in spelling, punctuation, a few words or a sentence; its note describes the setting, whose line breaks and type are not recorded.

The regions and lines of the scans were mostly marked in eScriptorium and converted from PAGE XML to TEI. The text was in part recognised automatically (HTR) and corrected against the scan, in part transcribed by hand. The advertisements published outside Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States, and a few from Germany, were transcribed from the scans, encoded and given their regions by a large language model (Claude, by Anthropic); their revision history says so. Until the editor has checked such an advertisement against the scan, status on its revisionDesc is unchecked; that of every other advertisement is checked. The topics of all advertisements were assigned by the same model.

correction.p: Errors of the original are not corrected but marked with sic.

normalization.p: Spelling and punctuation follow the original and are not normalised. Text set in capitals is often transcribed in mixed case and marked with the rendition #uc.

hyphenation.p: Hyphens at the end of a line are kept as printed.

segmentation.p: Every region of the original page is a div that points to its zone in the facsimile with facs. The lines of the original are marked with lb; the typography is recorded with rendition. The zones refer to the first graphic of a surface, the scan they were drawn on. Where the holding library serves the page through IIIF, a second graphic of the type IIIF gives that image and its size.

interpretation.p: Parts of an advertisement that concern other products than the Welte-Mignon are not transcribed but marked with gap, which describes them in a desc. Illustrations are described in figure. Persons are linked to the GND with corresp; firms are linked to the GND or, where it has no record of them, to Wikidata. Recurring arguments and motifs are marked as topics with ana on seg and figure, pointing to the taxonomy of topics. The taxonomy was induced by the language model in four blind readings of all advertisements, each in a different order and without knowledge of the editor's earlier taxonomy, which it replaced in October 2026; it keeps the topics that at least three of the readings found. The topics are an interpretation, assigned by whom resp says, so far all by the language model; the editor has not yet checked them.

stdVals.p: Dates of publication are given in ISO 8601 in when, as precisely as they are known.

taxonomy.desc: Topics: the recurring arguments and motifs of the advertisements, in their texts and in their pictures

category.desc: The ad claims that the playing of the artist is reproduced exactly, faithfully, naturally or completely, as "the actual playing" of the pianist. A bare "reproduces the playing of …" without such a qualifier does not count.
The ad names what is kept beyond the notes: touch, phrasing, pedalling, dynamics, tempo, shading, tone colour, or the individuality and characteristic style of each pianist.
The playing is preserved for ever or for future generations; the artists become immortal, and dead artists still play.

category.gloss: The great pianists in your home
category.desc: The famous pianists can be heard in your own home or on your own piano, at any time, as often as you wish, at your command ("The Master's Fingers on Your Piano", concerts at home).
The case, its design or period style; the instrument as an ornament of the room.
The instrument is framed as an invention: epoch-making, ingenious, the greatest of the age, a sensation, the newest thing.
The instrument is called perfect, the best, the finest, supreme or unsurpassed, or the culmination of a line of progress.

The ad explains or shows the technology: the recording process, the pneumatic or electric mechanism, the roll, the drive from a light socket, or it likens the recording to photography or the phonograph. A product label such as "electric reproducing piano" alone does not count.
The instrument remains an ordinary piano: it can be played by hand, the mechanism is invisible and leaves its look unchanged, it can be fitted to many makes of piano.

ab.hi:
Brings to your home the actual living perform-
ances of Hofmann, Lhevinne, Paderewski,
Bloomfield-Zeisler and
a hundred
other great
pianists.

p.seg:
The science of musical reproduction has progressed
through the various stages–experiment, medioc-
rity, excellence–but until the introduction of the
Welte-Mignon it has never reached supreme per-
fection. But today the science has reached its apex,
the goal has been attained and beyond the splendid
achievement realized in the Welte-Mignon it is im-
possible to go.

div.p:
The Welte-Mignon brings to the music-lover
the actual performances of every great living pian-
ist.
It perpetuates these performances so that fu-
ture generations will enjoy the music of our
present-day virtuosos when their personalities are
but misty memories.

What the Victor is doing for the famous singers
of the world the Welte-Mignon is accomplishing
for the pianists.
But with this difference: The
Victor registers the voice vibrations on the disc,
whereas the sensitive reproducing devices of the
Welte-Mignon are of such nature that every dupli-
cate performance IS MADE DIRECTLY ON THE
PIANO,
thereby reproducing in every detail of
touch, tone and technique the actual renditions of
the pianists, in every sense their original per-
formances.

The series of instruments containing the repro-
duction devices are the Welte-Mignon, as illustrated
above; the Steinway-Welte, an upright Steinway
piano combined with the Welte-Mignon, and the
Cabinet-Welte, which may be attached to any grand
or upright piano of any make.
